vignette:
He is a 69-year-old South Eastern Asian man who comes across as careful, soft-spoken, and deeply devoted to the children in his care. He has lived many years in the U.S. and works as a nanny, a job he took on after his wife died and the house became too quiet. In sessions, he speaks with a gentle steadiness, but his hands often twist together when he talks about the period when his young daughter became critically ill. That time still feels close to him, as if it happened yesterday.

The crisis begins when his child, still small and dependent on him for everything, develops a severe illness that progresses quickly and becomes life-threatening. At first, he thinks it is a fever that will pass. He remembers trying to remain calm so he would not frighten his wife or the child, but the child's breathing worsens, the hospital visits intensify, and the doctors speak in urgent, confusing phrases. He cannot understand why a healthy child can become so sick so fast. He sits in waiting rooms for hours, watching the clock and feeling his body tighten as each new update seems to carry the possibility of loss. He describes a growing sense of helplessness that becomes the central memory of that period: he is present, he is trying, but he cannot protect the person he loves most.

While his child is hospitalized, he stops sleeping in any meaningful way. Even now, he says he still wakes at the smallest sound, listening for breathing that is too shallow or too quiet. At the time, he stays on alert day and night, afraid that if he lets himself rest for even a moment, something irreversible will happen. He remembers standing by the bedside and studying every change in the child's face, the monitors, the nurses' expressions, searching for clues. He becomes consumed by responsibility and guilt, replaying ordinary moments from before the illness and wondering whether he missed a sign, whether he should have acted sooner, whether he somehow failed as a father. The questions do not lead anywhere, but they circle constantly.

The illness lasts long enough to reshape the whole family. His wife cries privately so the child will not see. He tries to be the one who remains solid, but inside he feels himself fraying. He notices that he starts flinching at hospital alarms, sudden phone calls, and any mention of fever, infection, or emergency care. He cannot tolerate seeing other children hooked to IVs or hearing parents speak casually about sickness. Even after his child survives and slowly recovers, relief does not arrive cleanly. Instead, he feels a strange mix of gratitude and fear, as if happiness is now always balanced on the edge of disaster. He keeps expecting the illness to return.

Over the years, the memory hardens rather than softens. He avoids medical television scenes and sometimes leaves the room when illness is discussed. He checks on the children he nannies with an intensity that can seem excessive to others: he watches their color, their energy, their appetite, their coughs. He is loving and attentive, but underneath that care is vigilance that never fully turns off. When one of the children he looks after gets sick, even with a minor cold, he is flooded with the same old terror. His chest tightens, his mind rushes ahead to worst-case scenarios, and he finds it difficult to breathe until he can be sure the child is safe. He has become known as dependable and nurturing, yet he privately carries the constant expectation that something beloved can be taken without warning.

His wife's death later deepens the sense that life removes people too quickly. He does not describe a single moment when everything changed; instead, he speaks of a long accumulating ache. He becomes more withdrawn, more easily startled, and more likely to sit alone after work instead of joining others. He has moments when he feels back in the hospital corridor, waiting for news, his body tense and ready for catastrophe. Even years later, he still has vivid images of his child's sick face and the sound of machines, and these memories arrive uninvited when he is trying to work, cook, or fall asleep.

What stands out is how much he continues to love and protect despite the fear. He shows up every day for other people's children, but he does so with a seriousness that seems to come from having once stood helplessly beside a hospital bed and promised himself he would never miss another warning sign.
